nameStory: Creeping lespedeza gets its name from its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit - it literally creeps along the forest floor rather than standing upright like many of its bush clover cousins. The genus name Lespedeza honors Vicente Manuel de Céspedes, an 18th-century Spanish governor of East Florida who supported botanical exploration.
description: Creeping lespedeza is a low-growing perennial wildflower that belongs to the legume family, making it a cousin to beans and peas. Unlike the upright bush clovers, this plant sends out trailing stems that can stretch up to 3 feet long, hugging the ground as they spread. It produces small purple or pink pea-like flowers from late spring through early fall, and like other legumes, it has the special ability to add nitrogen to the soil through its root system.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stems trail along the ground rather than standing upright, creating a sprawling mat that can spread several feet across. The stems feel somewhat wiry but flexible to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part clover-like leaves that noticeably get smaller as you move toward the stem tips. Each leaflet is oval-shaped with a smooth, soft texture and no teeth along the edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pea-like flowers in shades of purple, pink, or sometimes nearly white, typically arranged in small clusters. Each flower has the classic legume shape with an upper banner petal and lower keel.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened pods about the size of a lentil that contain just one or two seeds. The pods feel papery when mature and don't split open dramatically like some legumes.

habitat: Look for creeping lespedeza in partially shaded areas like open woodlands, forest clearings, and the edges of thickets where sunlight can still filter through. It prefers well-drained soils and often grows alongside other woodland wildflowers and native grasses. In New England, it's quite rare and most likely to be found in the southern portions of the region.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges in late spring, with fresh three-part leaves appearing along last year's stems or from the root system.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with small purple-pink flowers appearing in clusters. The trailing stems are most obvious now as they spread across the ground.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by small seed pods. Leaves may begin to yellow as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back, leaving only the root system alive underground to sprout again next spring.

funFact: This little ground-hugger is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only twice in recent botanical surveys, making it one of the most elusive native wildflowers in the region - you're more likely to spot a moose than find this creeping treasure!
confusionNotes: The trailing growth habit makes it easy to distinguish from other bush clovers, which all grow upright. It could be confused with wild strawberry when not in bloom, but strawberry has toothed leaf edges while creeping lespedeza's leaves are smooth, and strawberry has white flowers rather than purple-pink ones.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'bush' clover, creeping lespedeza doesn't form a bush at all - it's the rebel of the lespedeza family. Many gardeners are familiar with non-native lespedezas used for erosion control, but our native creeping species is much more subtle and environmentally valuable for native wildlife.
compareHints: While most of its lespedeza relatives like round-headed bush clover and violet bush clover grow upright in bushy clumps, creeping lespedeza is the ground-hugger of the family. Its trailing stems and progressively smaller leaves toward the stem tips are unique among New England's bush clovers. The flowers are similar in color to violet bush clover but much smaller and more scattered along the stems.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Round-headed bush clover stands out from its Lespedeza relatives by its distinctly round, compact flower heads - most other bush clovers have loose, elongated flower clusters or flowers scattered along the stems.
Among New England's bush clovers, hairy lespedeza stands out for its distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture covering the entire plant.
Among its bush clover relatives, violet bush clover stands out with its smooth (not hairy) stems and leaves, and its loose flower arrangement rather than dense round clusters.
Among New England's bush clovers, Chinese bushclover stands out for its silvery, densely hairy appearance and aggressive colonial growth habit.
Among New England's bush clovers, slender bush clover stands out for its delicate, wispy appearance with thin stems and small flower clusters.

Among its bush-clover relatives, tall bush-clover stands out with its reliably erect stems - round-headed bush clover has similar upright growth but denser, more rounded flower clusters, while violet bush clover and trailing lespedeza have more sprawling or leaning growth habits.
Among the many Lespedeza species, shrub lespedeza is unique in New England for its tall, shrubby growth habit - most other bush clovers in our region are low-growing or trailing plants.
Unlike its upright relatives like round-headed bush clover or hairy lespedeza that can reach several feet tall, trailing lespedeza never gets off the ground.
Among its bush clover relatives, narrow-leaved bush clover stands out for its distinctly slender leaflets and preference for wet soils.
Among the bush clovers in New England, violet bush clover stands out for its distinctly purple-violet flowers - most of its relatives have white, cream, or very pale pink blooms.
Among the lespedezas, Thunberg's is unique for its dramatic weeping form - most other bush clovers in New England grow upright or spreading but not with these long, graceful drooping branches.
Downy lespedeza stands out from other bush clovers in New England primarily by its extremely fuzzy, silvery appearance.
